title: Material criteria for angular-momentum transfer from twisted photons to photoelectrons
authors: A. A. Shchepkin, D. V. Karlovets
abstract: We study the material requirements for transferring the total-angular-momentum (TAM) projection of a twisted photon to the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of a photoelectron emitted from an $n$-type semiconductor surface. Within a single-valley effective-mass model of surface photoemission, we calculate OAM-resolved spectra for GaAs, InSb, $\mathrm{InAs}_{0.34}\mathrm{Sb}_{0.66}$, and $\mathrm{Hg}_{0.76}\mathrm{Cd}_{0.24}\mathrm{Te}$ irradiated by twisted photons with Laguerre--Gaussian--like momentum profile. The OAM transfer is characterized by the mean electron OAM, its root-mean-squared width, and the fraction of electrons with OAM-projection equal to the photon TAM-projection. Efficient transfer requires the transverse momentum of the conduction electron to be much smaller than the transverse momentum width of the photon, which favors low temperatures, small conduction-band effective masses, and shallow donor levels. GaAs is less favorable within the present model because of its larger effective mass and deeper donor levels. We also discuss the demanding photon-wave packet parameters, possible extensions to Dirac and Weyl semimetals, and post-emission OAM selection. Although the generation of vortex electrons with a vanishing OAM uncertainty via photoemission seems challenging, we argue that it is still possible to generate single-electron vortex states with a finite OAM dispersion.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes the conditions required for transferring the angular momentum carried by twisted photons into the orbital angular momentum of emitted photoelectrons from semiconductor surfaces. By calculating OAM-resolved spectra for several materials, the authors determined that low effective mass and shallow donor levels are crucial for efficient transfer. The findings guide the selection of optimal semiconductor materials for generating highly controlled electron angular momentum states.
main_problem: The study investigates the material requirements necessary for efficiently transferring the total-angular-momentum (TAM) projection from a twisted photon to the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of an emitted photoelectron.
main_result: Efficient OAM transfer is favored in materials with small conduction-band effective masses and shallow donor levels, while GaAs was found to be less favorable due to its larger effective mass and deeper donor levels.
method: The authors calculated OAM-resolved photoemission spectra using a single-valley effective-mass model for surface photoemission.
model_or_system: The system involves photoemission from n-type semiconductor surfaces (e.g., GaAs, InSb) irradiated by twisted photons, modeled using a single-electron Hamiltonian and projected onto Bessel states.
key_observables: Mean electron OAM, root-mean-squared (rms) OAM width, and the fraction of electrons matching the photon's TAM projection ($\eta_m$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures, small conduction-band effective masses, and shallow donor levels are critical for efficient transfer.
main_assumptions: The model neglects electron-electron, electron-phonon, and electron-impurity interactions, and assumes a flat, defect-free interface.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the geometry of the surface photoelectric effect, showing the semiconductor in the negative z-region and emission into the vacuum.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, details the theoretical model and calculations for various semiconductors, analyzes the dependence of OAM transfer on material parameters, and discusses future extensions to Dirac/Weyl semimetals.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics (twisted photons) with condensed matter physics (semiconductor photoemission), providing quantitative criteria for controlling electron angular momentum, which is relevant for advanced quantum sources and detectors.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Geometry of the surface photoelectric effect induced by a twisted photon. The semiconductor occupies the half-space z < 0, and the emitted electron propagates into the vacuum region z > 0.

Figure 2: OAM-resolved differential photoemission probability for GaAs at T = 2.5 K (top) and T = 4 K (bottom) for an incident twisted-photon state with ¯kz = −5 eV, σ⊥= 1 eV and σz = 2 eV. The photon TAM projections are mγ = 1, 5, 16 and 64. The finite thermal momentum of the initial electrons broadens the distribution away from the ideal selection rule le = mγ. The effect becomes particularly strong for large mγ.

Figure 3: OAM-resolved normalized differential photoemission probability for InSb, InAs0.34Sb0.66, and Hg0.76Cd0.24Te. The four columns correspond to the total angular-momentum projections of the incident twisted photon, mγ = 1, 5, 16, and 64, respectively, for ¯kz = −5 eV, σ⊥= 1 eV, σz = 2 eV. For each material, the upper and lower rows show the photoelectron OAM distributions at T = 0.5 K and T = 4 K, respectively. The pairs of rows from top to bottom correspond to InSb, InAs0.34Sb0.66, and Hg0.76Cd0.24Te. The dashed vertical lines indicate the desired OAM-transfer channel le = mγ.
